questions.question_text: Reading comprehension is:
options: The ability to read a text, understand it and interpret its meaning
questions.explanation: It involves understanding, interpreting and evaluating.

questions.question_text: The levels of comprehension are:
questions.explanation: Each goes deeper into the text.

questions.question_text: Literal comprehension means:
options: Understanding what is directly stated in the text
questions.explanation: The answers are found in the text.

questions.question_text: Inferential comprehension means:
options: Understanding ideas that are implied but not directly stated
questions.explanation: It requires reading between the lines.

questions.question_text: Critical reading means:
options: Evaluating the text for accuracy, bias, logic and purpose
questions.explanation: It questions what the author says.

questions.question_text: Skimming is:
options: Reading quickly to get the general idea of a text
questions.explanation: It is used for previewing material.

questions.question_text: Scanning is:
options: Reading quickly to find a specific piece of information, such as a name or number
questions.explanation: It is used with timetables and indexes.

questions.question_text: Skimming differs from scanning in that skimming looks for _____ and scanning looks for _____:
Intensive reading is:
options: Careful, detailed reading of a short text to understand it fully
questions.explanation: It is used for study and analysis.

questions.question_text: Extensive reading is:
options: Detailed study of a short text
Reading longer texts or many books for general understanding and enjoyment

questions.question_text: Intensive reading differs from extensive reading in that intensive reading is:
options: Detailed and slow, while extensive reading is broad and for pleasure

questions.question_text: Speed reading is:
questions.explanation: It uses techniques to reduce regression.

questions.question_text: SQ3R stands for:
questions.explanation: It is a study method for textbooks.

questions.question_text: A strategy of effective reading is:
To predict content before reading, you should:
options: Look at the title, headings, images and first lines
questions.explanation: It prepares the mind for the text.

questions.question_text: To annotate a text, you:
options: Underline key points and write brief notes in the margin

questions.question_text: To summarise a paragraph, you:
options: Identify the main idea and restate it briefly in your own words

questions.question_text: The meaning of an unknown word can be guessed by:
options: Using clues from the surrounding words and sentences

questions.question_text: Context clues include:
options: Definitions, synonyms, antonyms and examples in the sentence

questions.question_text: Knowing prefixes and roots helps in reading because:
options: They reveal the meaning of unfamiliar words, e.g., "un-" means not

questions.question_text: A tip to improve reading speed is:
options: Avoid subvocalisation and regression, and read in phrases

questions.question_text: Subvocalisation is _____, and regression is _____:
options: Silently pronouncing words while reading; going back to re-read words

questions.question_text: The genres of text include:
options: Fiction, non-fiction, poetry, drama and news

questions.question_text: A feature of fiction is that it:
options: Is an imaginative narrative with characters, plot and setting

questions.question_text: The elements of a story are:
options: Characters, setting, plot, conflict and theme
questions.explanation: Plot includes beginning, climax and resolution.

questions.question_text: A news report follows the inverted pyramid, which means:
options: The most important information comes first, followed by details
questions.explanation: It answers who, what, when, where, why.

questions.question_text: An editorial is:
options: An article expressing the opinion of the newspaper or editor on an issue

questions.question_text: Academic texts are characterised by:
options: Formal tone, specialised vocabulary and cited sources

questions.question_text: Business texts are characterised by:
options: Clear, concise, purposeful language and a practical focus
questions.explanation: They aim at action or decision.

questions.question_text: Business documents one may need to read include:
options: Reports, memos, emails, contracts and annual reports

questions.question_text: A report differs from a memo in that a report is:
options: A detailed, formal document, while a memo is a short internal communication

questions.question_text: An executive summary is:
options: A short overview of the main points of a report for busy readers

questions.question_text: To read an annual report, you should:
options: Start with the executive summary and chairman's message, then check financial statements and notes

questions.question_text: When reading a contract, you should:
options: Read carefully, focusing on obligations, rights, deadlines and penalties

questions.question_text: Characteristics of poetry include:
options: Rhythm, rhyme, imagery and compressed language

questions.question_text: Figurative language includes:
A feature of persuasive texts is that they:
options: Use reasons, emotional appeals and a call to action

questions.question_text: Blogs differ from academic articles in that blogs are:
options: Informal, personal and often opinion-based, while academic articles are formal and cited

questions.question_text: The difficulty of a text depends on:
options: Vocabulary, sentence length, structure and subject familiarity

questions.question_text: A basic reading level differs from an advanced reading level in that basic texts have:
options: Simple words and sentences, while advanced texts have complex vocabulary and ideas

questions.question_text: The role of vocabulary in comprehension is that:
options: A wide vocabulary makes it easier to understand texts

questions.question_text: Long and complex sentences affect comprehension by:
options: Making a text harder to follow

questions.question_text: Tone is:
options: The author's attitude toward the subject (e.g., formal, humorous, critical, optimistic, sarcastic)
questions.explanation: It is shown through word choice.

questions.question_text: The author's purpose can be to:
The tone of "The proposal is utterly ridiculous and a waste of time" is:
The tone of "We are delighted to announce our new scholarship programme" is:
A fact differs from an opinion in that a fact:
options: Can be verified, while an opinion is a personal belief

questions.question_text: "India's financial year starts on 1 April" is a:
"Online shopping is better than shopping in stores" is a:
"Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius at sea level" is a:
"Everyone should invest in mutual funds" is a:
The main idea of a passage is:
options: The central point the author wants to convey, usually found in the topic sentence
questions.explanation: Look at the first and last sentences.

questions.question_text: Supporting details are:
options: Facts, examples and explanations that support the main idea

questions.question_text: An inference is:
options: A conclusion drawn from clues in the text and prior knowledge
questions.explanation: E.g., wet roads suggest recent rain.

questions.question_text: From "Meera checked her watch every minute and kept staring at the door," we can infer that she was:
options: Anxious or impatient, waiting for someone

questions.question_text: From "The streets were empty, shops closed, and the sky was grey and heavy," we can infer that:
options: It was probably a holiday or a stormy day
It was a busy market day
questions.explanation: The details suggest quiet and bad weather.

questions.question_text: From "The CEO cancelled all meetings and spent the whole evening with the finance team," we can infer that:
options: There was an urgent financial issue

questions.question_text: "Reading between the lines" means:
options: Understanding implied meaning not directly stated

questions.question_text: Reference questions ask:
options: What a pronoun or phrase refers to in the text, e.g., "What does 'it' refer to?"
questions.explanation: They test understanding of links in the text.

questions.question_text: In "The manager told the clerk that he would be promoted," the pronoun "he" most likely refers to:
questions.explanation: The sentence is ambiguous; context decides.

questions.question_text: A True/False/Not Given question asks you to:
options: Decide whether the statement agrees with, contradicts or is not mentioned in the text
questions.explanation: "Not Given" means there is no information.

questions.question_text: To answer a multiple-choice comprehension question, you should:
options: Read the question first, find the evidence in the text and eliminate wrong options
questions.explanation: Check each option against the passage.

questions.question_text: To answer a short-answer question, you should:
options: Give a brief, direct answer based on the text, in your own words

questions.question_text: To write a summary of a passage:
options: Identify the main points and rewrite them concisely in your own words
questions.explanation: It should be about one-third of the length.

questions.question_text: A suitable title for a passage should:
options: Reflect the main idea and be short and catchy

questions.question_text: The steps in answering a comprehension passage are:
options: Read the passage, read the questions, locate evidence, answer and check

questions.question_text: From "Rohan arrived twenty minutes early, reviewed his notes calmly, greeted the receptionist politely, and answered each question with confidence," we can infer that Rohan was:
"The company's profit rose by 12% in the third quarter, mainly due to higher exports, although costs also increased by 5%." The profit growth was caused by:
The main idea of "Renewable energy, once considered expensive, is now the cheapest source of power in many regions" is:
options: Renewable energy has become the cheapest power source in many regions

questions.question_text: "Anita saved Rs 2,000 every month for five years. She then used the money to start a small tailoring unit." This shows that Anita is:
questions.explanation: She saved regularly and started a business.

questions.question_text: "Although the new app was popular, many users complained that it drained their phone batteries." The complaint was:
options: The app drained their phone batteries
questions.explanation: The complaint is the battery drain.

questions.question_text: "Due to heavy rainfall, the match was postponed to Sunday." The match was postponed because of:
"The librarian placed a finger on her lips and glared at the noisy students." She wanted them to:
In "Despite repeated warnings, the factory continued to dump waste into the river," "despite" shows:
options: Contrast: the action continued against warnings

questions.question_text: In "The manager's candid feedback surprised the team," "candid" means:
The antonym of "scarce" in "Water was abundant during the monsoon, though it was scarce in summer" is:
"Break the ice" in "He told a joke to break the ice at the meeting" means:
options: To ease tension and start conversation

questions.question_text: The phrasal verb "carry out" in "The team will carry out a survey" means:
questions.explanation: It means to perform a task.

questions.question_text: "Bottom line" in business reading means:
options: The last line of a page
The final outcome, especially net profit or the key conclusion

questions.question_text: When reading a graph or chart described in a text, you should:
options: Check the title, labels, units and trends before the details

questions.question_text: To read an email chain efficiently, you should:
options: Start with the latest message and scan earlier ones for context
questions.explanation: Check the subject and key actions.

questions.question_text: Reading helps improve writing by:
options: Exposing you to vocabulary, structures and styles

questions.question_text: The reliability of a source is evaluated by checking:
options: Author credibility, publication, date, evidence and bias

questions.question_text: Bias in a text is:
options: One-sided or prejudiced presentation; it can be detected by loaded words and missing viewpoints

questions.question_text: To read an editorial critically, you should:
options: Identify the writer's position, evidence and possible bias

questions.question_text: When facing an unfamiliar topic in a comprehension passage:
options: Rely on the text, not on prior knowledge, and use context to answer
questions.explanation: All answers are in the passage.

questions.question_text: Regular reading is important for business students because it:
options: Builds vocabulary, knowledge and analytical skills

questions.question_text: "The shop opens at 9 am and closes at 8 pm, except on Sundays when it stays closed." The shop is closed on:
Rs 2 lakh at 10% simple interest for two years gives interest of:
"Our latest model is lighter, faster and cheaper than its predecessor" is most likely:
The two aims of the new solar subsidy are:
options: To reduce electricity bills and cut carbon emissions

questions.question_text: "Few employees attended the training, though it was mandatory" implies that:
options: Many employees ignored a mandatory requirement

questions.question_text: The topic sentence in "Teamwork improves results. Members share ideas, divide tasks and support each other." is:
Headings and subheadings in a report:
options: Show the structure and help readers find information quickly

questions.question_text: To read a research abstract quickly, you should:
options: Focus on the purpose, method, findings and conclusion

questions.question_text: A main idea differs from a topic in that the main idea:
options: Is the point the author makes about the topic, while the topic is the subject

questions.question_text: Paraphrasing is:
options: Restating text in your own words while keeping the meaning, e.g., "The company is facing money problems"

questions.question_text: Signal words in a passage are:
options: Words like "however", "therefore" and "for example" that show relationships between ideas

questions.question_text: The sequence of events in a passage is:
options: The order in which events happen, shown by words like first, then, finally
questions.explanation: It matters in narratives and processes.

questions.question_text: Reading aloud helps comprehension by:
options: Slowing down, focusing attention and helping with pronunciation and rhythm
